newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Dublin-based futures exchange sees bright future.
newsitem.headline: Dublin-based futures exchange sees bright future.

text.p: Finex Europe, a unit of the New York Cotton Exchange (NYCE), sees a bright future ahead and expects European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) to add spice to its currency contracts.

"Finex is doing spectacularly at the end of 1996," NYCE president Joe O'Neill told Reuters. "We are looking to keep the same growth pattern in 1997 so, that means we are looking for tremendous growth next year."

Finex Europe managing director Hunt Taylor said a move towards a single currency in Europe was not a cause for concern for Finex as it merely meant a number of contracts would combine to create one very big contract.

"Some currencies will merge into a single currency, but that trading will consolidate into a mega contract, which is euro trading. It is not that any trading will go away, it will instead consolidate into a huge trading vehicle," Taylor said.

Finex Europe was set up in Dublin's International Financial Services Centre in 1994. Since its genesis, the facility's floor population has grown from seven firms and nine approved traders to 30 firms and 50 approved traders.
"We are trading a total of 22 futures and options contracts on the Dublin floor including dollar index futures and options, mark-based currency and dollar currency products," Taylor said.
Finex operates in conjunction with a sister operation in New York and when one closes, the other facility takes over to give round-the-clock service in futures and options trading.
Taylor said global foreign exchange markets turn over $1.2 trillion a day and Europe alone turns over $600 billion a day.
"In September, which is our benchmark at the moment, we turned over $1.0 billion for the currency complex, most of which comes out of Europe," he said.
The Dublin facility represents 50 to 70 percent of the total contracts trading in Finex on both sides of the Atlantic, NYCE president O'Neill said.
Taylor said the little start-up currencies exchange in Dublin is growing at triple digit rates when most of the foreign exchange markets are contracting because its markets are liquid.

"The fact that we combine the floor population with this block order pricing system where all the larger transactions are priced by interbank market markers means that we have evolved into one of the most liquid trading forums, despite our relative lack of size vis-a-vis our competition," Taylor said.
Taylor said some of the most sizeable markets in the industry are made at the Finex. "What it means in practical terms is that we can very quickly replicate what is going on in the cash market."
Finex is also gaining from changing macro-economic trends in Europe.

"Macro-economic trends in play in Europe right now are working to our advantage," Taylor said. "Credit has contracted dramatically in Europe so organisations that might have been able to secure interbank cash lines easily in 1993 are having a lot of trouble today," he said.

He said banks are finding that their credit committees are becoming increasingly conservative in terms of the types of exposures they are willing to carry on their books "...and that makes futures trading a very good alternative."
He said Finex was also picking up a lot of new business.

"We are getting new business from futures trading organisations who are interested in trading a broader range of products. Traditionally, they were constricted to trading futures for regulatory or credit reasons, and they traded the four majors that were available in Chicago (at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange)."
Taylor said now Finex has given them access on a regulated exchange to another six contracts.
"That business just was not being done anywhere before."
